query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An actively learned machine‐learning interatomic potential (MLIP), trained on a representative set of ab initio liquid and solid configurations, can replace traditional EAM references for high-entropy alloys at high melting temperatures to improve phase-space overlap and significantly reduce the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both liquid and solid states near their high melting temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace the standard EAM potential used in TOR-TILD with an MLIP (e.g., based on the DeepMD framework) that is trained via active learning on ab initio data capturing the rich atomic configurations of the liquid state.
generation.conditions: Applicable to refractory and complex high-entropy alloys (e.g., Nb-Mo-Ta type systems or similar multicomponent systems) at temperatures around 0.9–1.1 times their melting point.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLIP architecture and its active learning protocol serve as the mediator by integrating diverse atomic configurations from both liquid and solid states into the model.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly incorporating a wide range of ab initio configurations (especially from the liquid state) into its training set, the ML potential can more accurately represent the energetic landscape. This enhanced representation improves the reference-target phase-space overlap, leading to a smoother and shorter thermodynamic integration path compared to that obtained with EAM potentials, which are unable to capture the configurational complexity of the ab initio liquid.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermodynamic integration calculations will show a markedly reduced free-energy path mismatch (for instance, on the order of a 50% reduction) when using the MLIP compared to the traditional EAM references.
generation.baseline: Results obtained with TOR-TILD's EAM references, which exhibit larger thermodynamic integration path mismatches due to inadequate representation of the many atomic configurations in the liquid state.
generation.boundary: This intervention is likely effective only for high-complexity, multicomponent systems at temperatures near melting. Its efficacy may be limited for simpler alloys or systems where the atomic configuration diversity is not as pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in mismatch is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition, training set quality, and temperature. The predicted ~50% reduction serves as a rough estimate based on analogous studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel thermodynamic integration simulations on a selected multicomponent high-entropy alloy (e.g., a Nb-Mo-Ta-based system) at temperatures around its melting point. One set of simulations should use the traditional EAM-based TOR-TILD reference, and another set should use the actively learned MLIP. The free-energy integration paths of both methods are to be compared.
measurements: Free-energy differences along the integration paths
Quantitative metrics of phase-space overlap between the reference and target configurations
Statistical comparison of path smoothness and mismatch values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP-based thermodynamic integration does not yield a statistically significant reduction (approximately 50% or more) in path mismatch and fails to show improved phase-space overlap compared to the EAM reference, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The melting temperature together with supercooling and superheating temperatures of a number of high-entropy carbonitrides (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x with different concentrations of carbon substituted by nitrogen are calculated. The deep learning DeepMD potential is trained on the number of DFT calculations in order to accurately describe both the liquid and solid phases of the considered high-entropy carbonitrides. A new computational procedure is developed and applied to determine the melting hysteresis and melting temperature of HECN using active learning techniques. Heating and cooling curves for HECNs are calculated and carefully analyzed in order to determine the main trends in changes of melting temperatures with respect to nitrogen content. Pair correlation analysis is employed to explain the enhancement of the melting temperature of carbonitrides with small amounts of nitrogen. The obtained data indicates the potential of applications of high-entropy carbonitrides as promising hard and refractive materials for protective coatings of various equipment which operates at extreme conditions.
